Dragos also clarifies an operational point that is easy to miss in superficial retellings of the incident. In electric systems, loss of communications does not usually cause immediate shutdown. A device that loses connectivity often continues operating locally, but it can no longer be monitored or controlled remotely. This is why the power stayed on even though key OT and communications equipment had been compromised. Dragos therefore treats the incident as a serious OT intrusion with limited immediate physical effect, not as a failed or trivial attack. 

The brief further argues that the December 2025 operation represents both continuity and evolution relative to earlier ELECTRUM operations. Continuity lies in the use of destructive tooling, wipers, and attacks on communications infrastructure. Evolution lies in the shift from centralized control points, such as those targeted in Ukraine in 2015 and 2016, toward the distributed edge of the grid, meaning RTUs and communication systems spread across many smaller generation sites. Dragos assesses with moderate confidence that ELECTRUM was responsible, while also noting that the observed impact appears more opportunistic and less fully prepared than the earlier Ukraine operations.

This perspective sharpens the strategic meaning of the case. The Polish incident was not merely an enterprise compromise that happened to touch energy companies. It was an attack on the digital coordination fabric of distributed generation. The core lesson is that a modern grid does not need to lose its transmission backbone to suffer operationally relevant cyber sabotage. It is enough for an adversary to degrade visibility, telemetry, remote control, and restoration capability across enough distributed sites at the same time. 

[^poland-energy-sector-cyberattack-2025-DR26]: See Dragos’s public summary of the report: [Poland Power Grid Attack Targets Distributed Energy Resources](https://www.dragos.com/blog/poland-power-grid-attack-electrum-targets-distributed-energy-2025).

## Why the case matters

The Polish incident matters because it compresses several assumptions about energy cybersecurity into a single, well documented case and shows that many of them are no longer defensible. It demonstrates that operationally significant disruption can be achieved without causing a national blackout, without deploying highly specialized ICS malware at every stage, and without compromising the transmission backbone. The attacker was able to produce meaningful effects by targeting the digital coordination layer of distributed generation: remote access paths, telecontrol devices, communications infrastructure, domain services, and management surfaces that were easier to reach than the physical process itself.

That is the first major lesson. In energy systems, the **threshold for serious impact is lower than many discussions still imply**. A plant or portfolio does not need to stop generating for the attack to matter. It is enough that operators lose visibility, lose remote control, and lose confidence in the integrity of the devices that connect generation assets to the wider grid. Once those functions are degraded across many sites at once, the attacker has already created an operational problem, a regulatory problem, and a strategic signal.

The second lesson concerns distributed energy itself. Wind, solar, and CHP assets connected through remote telemetry and supervisory infrastructure are often treated as too small, too fragmented, or too peripheral to be systemically attractive. The Polish case shows the opposite. Their very number, geographic spread, and dependence on remote access make them suitable targets for a coordinated campaign. What looks like **decentralization from an electrical perspective can still be concentration from a cyber perspective** if dozens of sites share the same perimeter technologies, the same access patterns, the same administrative shortcuts, and the same weakly governed OT components.

The third lesson is that the **decisive weaknesses were largely architectural and operational**, not exotic. Exposed VPNs, missing multifactor authentication, reused credentials, permissive firewall configurations, default accounts on OT devices, insecure management protocols, weak firmware integrity protections, and poor recovery design were enough to enable sabotage at scale. That matters because it means the case cannot be dismissed as the product of rare zero days or uniquely sophisticated tooling. The uncomfortable implication is that similar outcomes are plausible anywhere comparable patterns exist.

Finally, the incident matters because it marks a strategic shift in how energy disruption can be pursued. Previous landmark grid attacks were associated with centralized control points and more obvious attempts to produce immediate outage effects. Poland shows a different model: attack the distributed edge, degrade the communications and supervision fabric, damage what is reachable, and impose operational stress **without necessarily crossing the threshold into catastrophic national disruption**. That model is more scalable, more deniable, and in some contexts politically more usable.

What Poland exposed, then, was not just a successful campaign against a set of organizations. It exposed a structural reality of modern power systems: as generation becomes more distributed, cyber fragility can also become more distributed, and **if that fragility is not governed deliberately, it can accumulate quietly across many small sites until it becomes strategically significant**. 

## Personal considerations: why this case matters to me in the Italian context

### Why the Polish case does not feel remote

What makes the Polish case especially relevant to me is that I do not read it as a remote anomaly. I see the same structural pattern in Italy, even if the geopolitical position, the regulatory environment, and the generation mix are not identical. The common pattern is not a specific threat actor or a specific device model. It is the combination of distributed sites, heavy dependence on remote access, edge devices that concentrate trust and reachability, heterogeneous OT components with uneven hardening, and organizational fragmentation between owners, EPCs, integrators, vendors, and O&M providers.

This is exactly the environment in which a large share of today’s renewable and hybrid energy systems is being designed and deployed. A modern plant is no longer just an electrical installation that happens to contain some digital components. It is, in substance, a **distributed cyber physical operating system** whose physical assets are coordinated, supervised, updated, dispatched, diagnosed, and sometimes even commercially optimized through remote digital relationships. The plant’s true attack surface therefore does not coincide with the visible field equipment taken one by one. It is not just the inverter, or the turbine, or the RTU, or the firewall considered in isolation. It is the **entire graph of trust, access, delegation, and dependency** that binds those components to remote operators, O&M teams, vendor support channels, dispatch and telecontrol interfaces, aggregators, cloud platforms, market systems, data concentrators, and third party maintenance paths.

That is the crucial shift in perspective. The plant is no longer only what is physically installed inside the fence. It is also the **extended digital ecosystem that is allowed to observe it, manage it, patch it, configure it, optimize it, and sometimes override it**. Every one of those relationships is operationally useful, but every one of them is also a potential attack path, a privilege boundary, or a latent failure mode. Once this is understood, the Polish incident stops looking like an outlier produced by unusual circumstances and starts looking like a highly legible warning. It becomes recognizable as the kind of event that can emerge wherever distributed assets are connected faster than the surrounding architecture of trust is deliberately governed.

### Why I use enterprise architecture and IEC 62443 at design time

This is also why I do not treat **enterprise architecture** and **IEC 62443** as paperwork to be added after engineering choices have already been made. I use them at design time because that is the most cost effective place to solve the problem. If segmentation, conduits, identity boundaries, remote access patterns, logging points, recovery paths, and administrative domains are decided only after procurement and deployment, the organization pays twice: first for a fast but fragile implementation, and then again for compensating controls, redesign, and operational friction. By contrast, when these choices are made in the architecture phase, security becomes a property of the system shape rather than a collection of late exceptions.

That distinction matters economically as much as technically. A **defensible architecture is not necessarily a more expensive architecture**. Very often it is simply a more explicit one. The cost effective move is to define from the beginning which functions belong in which zones, which communications are actually required, which identities are allowed to traverse which boundaries, how vendor access is brokered, what must be logged outside the local device, and what recovery baseline must exist if a field component is bricked or reset. The Polish incident shows what happens when those questions are left implicit: the attacker discovers the real architecture before the owner has fully governed it.

From this perspective, IEC 62443 is useful not because it is fashionable or because it can be cited in a checklist, but because it provides a disciplined way to convert these problems into design decisions. Zones and conduits force explicit trust boundaries. The foundational requirements force discipline around identification and authentication, restricted data flow, system integrity, and timely response to events. In practical terms, that means remote access cannot simply terminate _somewhere in OT_; management interfaces cannot remain reachable by convenience; default credentials and legacy services cannot survive commissioning; and restoration cannot depend on improvised field work after the incident has already destroyed the evidence.

### IEC 62443 reading of the Polish failure modes

The Polish case can also be read as a compact demonstration of why IEC 62443 is useful at design time. The standard is not important here as a formal citation exercise. Its value is that it **forces the architect to translate vague security concerns into concrete design properties**: zones, conduits, restricted data flows, identity boundaries, system integrity, monitoring, recovery, and lifecycle governance.

The table below maps the **main failure modes visible in the Polish incident to the corresponding IEC 62443 design logic**. The purpose is not to claim that formal compliance alone would have prevented the attack. It is more precise to say that an architecture genuinely designed according to IEC 62443 principles would have removed or weakened several of the attacker’s shortest paths to impact.

| Failure mode visible in the Polish case | IEC 62443 design concept | Practical architectural implication |
|---|---|---|
| Internet exposed VPN became the entry point into renewable site environments | Zones and conduits | Remote access should terminate in a controlled access zone, not directly into OT or mixed management networks. |
| FortiGate administrative control allowed the attacker to expand reach across segregated subnets | Restricted data flow and non-bypassable enforcement points | VLANs alone are not enough. Inter-zone traffic must be controlled by explicit policy enforcement points whose compromise does not silently collapse the whole zone model. |
| Missing multifactor authentication and reused credentials enabled scalable access across sites | Identification and authentication control | Remote access must use individual accounts, MFA, site-specific authorization, credential rotation, and ideally privileged access management for administrative paths. |
| Default credentials on RTUs, HMIs, relays, and serial device servers enabled direct device compromise | Account management and secure commissioning | Commissioning must include removal or disabling of default credentials, creation of accountable role-based access, and verification that vendor defaults are not left active. |
| OT management interfaces were reachable once the attacker gained network access | Least functionality and management plane isolation | Web, SSH, FTP, RDP, SMB, and firmware update interfaces should be reachable only from an engineering or maintenance zone, never from general remote access paths. |
| Legacy or unnecessary services such as FTP were available on protection devices | Least functionality | Services that are not operationally required must be disabled. If they are required for maintenance, they must be isolated, monitored, and opened only under controlled conditions. |
| Corrupted firmware was uploaded to RTUs | System integrity and controlled change | Firmware update paths must be authenticated, authorized, logged, and integrity checked. Where signed firmware is not available or not enabled, architecture must compensate by isolating the update interface. |
| Windows HMIs could be accessed and prepared for remote execution through RDP, SMB, and local administrator credentials | Host hardening and execution control | OT Windows hosts require hardening baselines, local administrator control, restricted inbound services, application allowlisting, and monitored administrative access. |
| Serial device servers were reset, reconfigured, and assigned unreachable IP addresses | Configuration management and recovery engineering | Field device configurations must be backed up, versioned, and restorable. Recovery should not depend on manual rediscovery of device state after destructive action. |
| Factory reset of FortiGate devices hindered recovery and erased local traces | Security monitoring and protected logging | Security logs must be exported to protected collectors outside the local device. A perimeter device must not be the only place where evidence of its own compromise exists. |
| Multi-site similarity made the attack repeatable across distributed assets | Security lifecycle and governance across the fleet | Standardization must not mean identical weakness. Fleet architecture should standardize secure patterns, not shared credentials, shared exposure, or repeated misconfigurations. |
| Limited OT visibility made it difficult to determine the full operational scope of adversary action | OT network visibility and timely response | Operators need visibility into OT traffic, commands, configuration changes, and remote access sessions before the incident occurs, because much of the evidence is transient. |
| Restoration depended on damaged or reconfigured field devices across multiple remote sites | Resilience and incident response readiness | Incident response must include golden configurations, tested restoration playbooks, spare device strategy, and prioritization rules for simultaneous multi-site recovery. |

The most important point is that IEC 62443 changes the topology of the attack graph. Without it, the attacker can move from remote access to perimeter device control, from perimeter control to OT reachability, from OT reachability to device management, and from device management to destructive action. With it, those transitions become explicit boundaries that must be crossed, authenticated, logged, justified, and constrained.

This is why IEC 62443 is most valuable before the plant is built. Once the system is already deployed, the owner is forced to retrofit controls around decisions that may already be structurally wrong. At design time, the same controls can be expressed as architecture: which zones exist, which conduits are allowed, which identities may cross them, which management interfaces are reachable, where evidence is stored, and how damaged devices are restored.

### Structural compliance by construction

This approach also has an important secondary effect: it tends to align the plant with the direction of regulation before the regulation arrives in its most detailed and most enforceable form. I would not call that _automatic compliance_ in a literal sense, because compliance always requires documentation, evidence, procedures, governance, and often formal role assignment. But I would call it **structural compliance by construction**. If the system is architected with explicit segmentation, secure remote access, asset accountability, monitoring, controlled change, and recovery engineering, then the gap between technical reality and regulatory expectation becomes much smaller.

This matters because the regulatory trajectory is no longer generic. It is becoming layered, cumulative, and increasingly specific at both system and product level. The result is that the technical decisions made during plant and interface design are progressively less separable from legal and regulatory obligations.

### The national layer: NIS2 and PSNC are converging, not diverging

At the national level, the relevance to the Polish case is not abstract. The attack documented by CERT Polska is exactly the kind of event that exposes why cyber governance for energy and industrial operators can no longer be treated as a secondary compliance exercise. It combines destructive intent, compromise of remote access paths, cross domain movement between IT and OT, and operational impact below the threshold of a nationwide blackout. In Italy, that same class of risk now sits inside a regulatory environment that is becoming denser and more explicit, not looser.

The first point is that the Italian transposition of NIS2 is already in force. **Decreto Legislativo 4 settembre 2024, n. 138** was published on 1 October 2024 and took effect on 16 October 2024[^poland-energy-sector-cyberattack-2025-138]. That matters here because NIS2 is not just about generic cybersecurity maturity. It is about forcing operators of essential and important entities to treat cyber risk, incident management, supply chain exposure, and continuity as governed management obligations rather than discretionary technical choices.

The second point is that this decree does not replace or supersede the **Perimetro di Sicurezza Nazionale Cibernetica**. The PSNC was established earlier and remains structurally important for systems tied to national strategic interests.[^poland-energy-sector-cyberattack-2025-PSNC] This is directly relevant to the logic of the article because the Polish case shows how systems that may appear operationally peripheral when considered site by site can become strategically relevant when attacked in coordination. The Italian framework is moving in the same conceptual direction: it narrows the distance between _technical infrastructure_ and _nationally significant infrastructure_ by treating certain digital systems, services, and interconnections as part of a higher consequence security perimeter.

The third and most important point is that **NIS2 and PSNC are converging, not diverging**. Article 33 of the Italian NIS2 transposition explicitly coordinates the two regimes by recognizing that, for systems already covered by the Perimetro, PSNC obligations on cyber risk management and incident notification are considered at least equivalent to the corresponding NIS2 obligations[^poland-energy-sector-cyberattack-2025-article33]. That is not a bureaucratic detail. It means that the direction of travel is toward a more integrated and less permissive model in which organizations cannot rely on fragmented interpretations of _which rule really applies_. From the standpoint of a plant owner, operator, or architect, the message is clear: the same architectural weaknesses highlighted by the Polish incident, especially around remote access, segmentation, trust boundaries, and recovery readiness, are increasingly becoming relevant both as technical exposures and as formal governance failures.

This is why the national layer matters so much to the argument of the article. The Polish incident is a warning that distributed energy and industrial systems can become operationally significant targets without first becoming _big critical infrastructure_ in the traditional centralized sense. The Italian response, through NIS2 and the continuing force of PSNC, points in the same direction: cyber resilience is being treated less as an optional quality of implementation and more as an expected property of strategically relevant systems and services. ACN’s own public positioning reflects this shift by presenting the NIS framework as fully in force and by identifying the Agency as the competent authority and single point of contact for the regime[^poland-energy-sector-cyberattack-2025-acn-nis].

[^poland-energy-sector-cyberattack-2025-acn-nis]: ACN states that the new NIS regime has been in force since 16 October 2024 and that ACN is the competent NIS authority and single point of contact. See the official NIS portal: [NIS - Network Information Security](https://www.acn.gov.it/portale/nis).

[^poland-energy-sector-cyberattack-2025-138]: The Italian transposition of NIS2 is **Decreto Legislativo 4 settembre 2024, n. 138**, published in *Gazzetta Ufficiale* on 1 October 2024 and in force from 16 October 2024. Official text: [Gazzetta Ufficiale](https://www.gazzettaufficiale.it/eli/id/2024/10/01/24G00155/SG).

[^poland-energy-sector-cyberattack-2025-PSNC]: The **Perimetro di Sicurezza Nazionale Cibernetica** was established by **Decreto-Legge 21 settembre 2019, n. 105**, then converted with modifications by **Legge 18 novembre 2019, n. 133**. Its incident notification and security measures were further operationalized through **DPCM 14 aprile 2021, n. 81**, in force from 26 June 2021. See the official publication of the implementing regulation: [Gazzetta Ufficiale](https://www.gazzettaufficiale.it/eli/id/2021/06/11/21G00089/SG).

[^poland-energy-sector-cyberattack-2025-article33]: Article 33 of **Decreto Legislativo n. 138/2024** coordinates NIS2 with the PSNC framework by treating Perimetro obligations on cyber risk management and incident notification as at least equivalent for the systems already covered by that regime. Official text: [Gazzetta Ufficiale](https://www.gazzettaufficiale.it/eli/id/2024/10/01/24G00155/SG).

### The grid code layer: what is already in force, and what is tightening further

At the energy specific layer, precision matters. The **Terna Grid Code** is already the governing framework for the transmission system and for the technical conditions under which plants, data acquisition systems, and defense related devices interface with Terna.[^poland-energy-sector-cyberattack-2025-Terna] But within that framework, it is important not to confuse three different things: the _current requirements already in force_, the _new revision path now visible in Terna’s update documents_, and the broader _direction of tightening_ that emerges when those texts are read together.

[^poland-energy-sector-cyberattack-2025-Terna]: Terna publishes the Grid Code (*Codice di Rete*) and its annexes as the governing technical framework for the national transmission system. The official annex list includes **A.13 _Criteri di connessione al sistema di controllo di Terna_** and **A.69 _Criteri di connessione degli impianti di produzione al sistema di difesa di Terna_**. See Terna’s official Grid Code page: [Codice di Rete Italiano](https://www.terna.it/it/sistema-elettrico/codici-rete/codice-rete-italiano).

#### What is already present in the current framework

Even in the current published version of **Annex A.13**, cybersecurity is not absent. The annex already contains a dedicated security chapter and already requires, among other things, protection and monitoring of communications toward Terna, logical segregation of networks and channels used for data exchange with Terna, prompt reporting of security incidents affecting the communication channel, VPN protection for acquisition systems that use intranet type communications, a VPN terminator on the owner side capable of segregating the network in which RTUs are present, security logs with synchronized timestamps, at least six months of log retention, and mutual authentication measures between the owner and Terna[^poland-energy-sector-cyberattack-2025-a13-current].

[^poland-energy-sector-cyberattack-2025-a13-current]: Current published Annex A.13: [Criteri di connessione al sistema di controllo di Terna](https://download.terna.it/terna/Allegato%20A.13%20%E2%80%93%20Criteri%20di%20connessione%20al%20sistema%20di%20controllo%20di%20Terna_8d7b56b4664fa83.pdf).

That point is important because it means the baseline is not starting from zero. Telecontrol and telemetry connections toward Terna are already treated as security relevant interfaces, not as purely functional transport paths.

#### What the new A.13 update makes clearer and stricter

Where the tightening becomes visible is in the **updated A.13 markup document**, which shows Terna moving from a relatively compact security chapter to a broader and more explicit cybersecurity framework. The updated text introduces a dedicated **Cyber Security** section structured around topics such as **asset inventory and third parties**, **cybersecurity monitoring and incident management**, **malware protection and traffic isolation**, **authentication and authorization**, **communications security and cryptography**, **packet filtering**, **patching**, **logging**, and **backup and restore**.[^terna-annex-a13-markup-structure]

[^terna-annex-a13-markup-structure]: [PDF](https://download.terna.it/terna/A13_Criteri_collegamento_Sistema_controllo_markup_8de0a841e7d100e.pdf)

The updated text also makes several obligations more explicit and more operational. It requires the plant owner to keep updated and consultable inventories of digital assets attached to the interconnection infrastructure, to maintain a 24x7 point of contact, to notify Terna of security events within **four hours** of detection when they may affect connected devices, communications infrastructure, Terna related information, or even supply chain events relevant to the interconnection, to ensure anti malware protection on IT, OT, IoT, and mobile devices, to isolate traffic between VPNs, to use robust credentials including examples such as **MFA**, to prepare for **IEC 62351** secure communications, to apply security patches at least **semiannually**, and to implement backup and restore procedures.

So the direction of travel is clear. The newer A.13 text does not merely repeat the older security concepts. It **broadens them, operationalizes them, and turns them into a more explicit lifecycle discipline** for the infrastructure that connects the plant to Terna’s systems.

This is already a significant architectural message. It means that cyber requirements are not only imposed later through generic corporate policy or audit language. They are increasingly embedded into the very conditions under which telemetry and telecontrol can be connected to the transmission side. The practical implication is that the connection architecture itself must now be designed to sustain asset visibility, segmented trust boundaries, secure remote access, incident response coordination, evidence retention, and recoverability.

#### The same tightening logic is visible in A.69

This becomes even more relevant when one looks at **Annex A.69**, which governs the connection of production plants to Terna’s defense system. In its current logic, A.69 already depends on A.13, because the telecontrol and data connection criteria of A.13 form part of the technical environment within which defense related interfaces operate.

But the newer **A.69 revision text** shows the same direction of tightening more explicitly. The updated text contains its own **Cyber Security** chapter, structured around **monitoring and threat detection**, **secure traffic isolation**, **authentication and authorization**, **traffic encryption**, **access controls and packet filtering**, **patching**, and **backup and restore**.[^poland-energy-sector-cyberattack-2025-69]

[^poland-energy-sector-cyberattack-2025-69]: [PDF](https://download.terna.it/terna/Allegato_A.69_8ddd426e0f51f03.pdf)

In addition, the revised A.69 text links cyber discipline directly to the integrated telecommunications architecture. It states that where the data connection system is integrated for A.69 purposes and also for A.7 and or A.13 purposes, continuity of telecontrol flows must be preserved throughout preparation, testing, and commissioning, and it imposes architectural consequences such as common communication technology constraints, readdressing of field devices, and the need to review the data network architecture when field devices other than RTUs and UPDM are used.

#### The actual direction of tightening

The most precise way to state the issue, then, is this: **Terna’s current framework already contains cyber relevant obligations, but the newer A.13 and A.69 texts show a clear move toward a more explicit, more granular, and more enforceable cybersecurity model at the plant to Terna interface**. The direction is not toward looser interoperability by default. It is toward tighter governance of communications, assets, authentication, logging, patching, and recovery, with increasing emphasis on the whole interconnection chain rather than on the mere existence of a data link.

### The product layer: the Cyber Resilience Act and CEI 0-16 are raising the baseline

In parallel, the product security baseline is tightening as well. At EU level, the **Cyber Resilience Act**, Regulation (EU) **2024/2847**, introduces horizontal cybersecurity requirements for products with digital elements, meaning hardware and software connected directly or indirectly to a device or network. The regulation entered into force on 10 December 2024. Its general application is staged, with the main obligations applying from 11 December 2027, while the reporting obligations for actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents begin earlier, from 11 September 2026.[^poland-energy-sector-cyberattack-2025-CRA]

[^poland-energy-sector-cyberattack-2025-CRA]: The **Cyber Resilience Act**, Regulation (EU) 2024/2847, entered into force on 10 December 2024. The main obligations apply from 11 December 2027, while the reporting obligations under Article 14 apply earlier, from 11 September 2026. See the European Commission’s summary: [Cyber Resilience Act](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/cyber-resilience-act).

This does not replace system architecture obligations, but it materially changes the product side expectations placed on vendors supplying connected components into energy systems. It pushes security requirements upstream, toward the design, development, lifecycle management, and incident reporting responsibilities of the product manufacturer.

The same tightening is visible in the Italian sector specific technical domain. **CEI 0-16 Variant V5** explicitly requires, for the **Controllore Centrale di Impianto (CCI)** as a whole, conformity to **IEC 62443-4-1** and **IEC 62443-4-2**. The text requires overall certification at **Capability Security Level 1**, together with additional assessment expectations for higher minimum levels on specific foundational requirements, in particular **FR1**, **FR2**, **FR3**, and **FR7**.[^poland-energy-sector-cyberattack-2025-CEI] This is not a generic invocation of good practice. It is a concrete sign that product and interface security expectations are being written into the technical rules of grid connected equipment.

[^poland-energy-sector-cyberattack-2025-CEI]: [PDF](https://static.ceinorme.it/strumenti-online/doc/26009.pdf)

### What this means in practice

Taken together, these layers point in the same direction. **NIS2, PSNC, the CRA, the Terna Grid Code, and CEI 0-16** are converging on one practical message: **remote telemetry, dispatch, and control interfaces can no longer be engineered as operational conveniences and justified later**. They must be designed from the outset as critical infrastructure surfaces.

This is why, for me, the lesson of the Polish case is straightforward. The right response is not to bolt more controls around the edges of an already ambiguous design. It is to design plants, substations, and remote operational ecosystems so that the most dangerous shortcuts are unavailable by default. That is what enterprise architecture is for at this level: not abstract modeling, but the deliberate shaping of trust, authority, and failure modes before those choices harden into expensive operational debt.

And this is the deeper reason I consider an architecture first, **IEC 62443 informed approach** to be the optimal balance between security and cost. It is cheaper to decide correctly than to retrofit under pressure. It is cheaper to standardize secure remote access than to investigate a fleet wide credential problem. It is cheaper to isolate management planes than to discover during an incident that a firewall configuration was the real crown jewel. It is cheaper to design for evidentiary logging and deterministic recovery than to rebuild dozens of sites with partial visibility after destructive actions have already occurred. In critical infrastructure, good architecture is not the opposite of cost effectiveness. It is usually the only durable form of it.

## Conclusions

The December 2025 cyberattack on Poland’s energy sector should be read as more than a national incident report and more than a malware case study. It is a reference event for the next phase of energy cybersecurity. Its real importance lies in showing that coordinated cyber sabotage of distributed generation does not require spectacular novelty. It requires enough understanding of how modern plants are actually operated, enough reach into the edge devices that mediate trust and control, and enough operational discipline to turn repeated weaknesses into repeatable disruption.

That is why the case is strategically important. It shifts attention away from the old intuition that grid cyber risk is concentrated only in major control centers and transmission assets. Those remain critical, but they are no longer the whole picture. The distributed edge of the grid now matters because that is where scale, remote access, operational heterogeneity, and inconsistent security investment meet. In such an environment, systemic relevance can emerge from the synchronized compromise of many small or medium assets that would not appear decisive in isolation.

The Polish incident also sharpens a more general principle. In critical infrastructure, the most dangerous vulnerabilities are often not the most technically exotic ones. They are the ones that have been normalized into operations: shared credentials, overprivileged perimeter devices, weak separation between remote access and administration, opaque vendor pathways, incomplete logging, and recovery models that depend on assumptions of benign failure rather than hostile interference. Once those become routine, the attacker does not have to invent a new path. The path is already there, waiting to be used.

For Italy, and more broadly for European operators living through the energy transition, the lesson is immediate. The expansion of distributed energy cannot be treated as only a capacity, market, and interconnection problem. It is also a problem of cyber architecture. If the digital operating model of distributed generation is designed as a convenience layer around electrical assets, then the attack surface scales faster than resilience. If instead it is designed from the beginning as critical infrastructure, then many of the attack paths visible in Poland become harder, noisier, slower, and more recoverable.

That is the point at which the Polish case becomes constructive rather than merely alarming. It gives operators, engineers, regulators, and owners a very clear warning, but also a very clear design agenda. The objective is not abstract _more security_. The objective is to make sure that remote access, dispatch interfaces, telemetry paths, OT management surfaces, and restoration processes are governed as part of the plant’s essential architecture. Once that is done, compliance with tightening Italian and European requirements becomes less of a late-stage burden and more the formal expression of choices that were already technically correct.

The deepest conclusion, then, is simple. The future risk to energy systems will not be determined only by how much renewable capacity is added, but by how that capacity is digitally organized. The Polish incident shows what happens when distributed generation is operationally connected faster than it is architecturally governed. The real strategic response is to reverse that sequence.

## Update, August 2026: the private APN attack path into a second CHP plant

On 8 August 2026, CERT Polska published a follow-up to its January incident report. The new analysis materially expands the reconstruction of the 29 December 2025 campaign: a **second, smaller combined heat and power plant**, supplying heat to approximately 50,000 residents, was also attacked that morning. More importantly, the investigation reconstructed an attack path that had not been visible in the original report. The attacker appears to have moved from a compromised wind farm, through a cellular router, into a **DSO-managed private APN**, then through a PLC connected to that APN into the second CHP plant's OT network. CERT Polska states that, to the best of its knowledge, this is the first observed real-world cyberattack in which a private APN was used in this way to gain access to an OT network.[^the-december-2025-cyberattack-on-polands-energy-sector-cert-polska-follow-up-2026]

This changes the architectural reading of the December incident in an important way. The original report already showed how weaknesses at individual grid connection points could be scaled across many renewable facilities. The follow-up shows something more systemic: **communications infrastructure intended to connect geographically distributed field assets can itself become a lateral-movement fabric between otherwise unrelated operational environments**. The significant boundary was therefore not only between the Internet and each plant. It was also between each field endpoint and the private telecommunications network to which that endpoint had been granted access.[^the-december-2025-cyberattack-on-polands-energy-sector-cert-polska-follow-up-2026]

### From a compromised wind farm into the private APN

The starting point was one of the wind farms already covered by the initial investigation. As described earlier in this article, the attacker had obtained access to a FortiGate appliance functioning as VPN concentrator and firewall. Inside that wind farm network was a **Teltonika RUTX50 cellular router** used for communication through a private APN operated by the DSO. The DSO's technical requirement that communication with the RTU use a serial protocol had been respected: the cellular router was connected to the RTU through an RS485 serial interface. At the same time, however, the router also had an Ethernet interface connected to a VLAN behind the compromised FortiGate.[^the-december-2025-cyberattack-on-polands-energy-sector-cert-polska-follow-up-2026]

That second interface was decisive. The Teltonika device exposed web administration and SSH services on its LAN side. Its original default password had been changed during commissioning, so this was not another simple default-credential case. CERT Polska could not determine how the attacker obtained the replacement password, nor could it establish whether a vulnerability in the router had been exploited. What investigators could establish was that the attacker logged into the router repeatedly over SSH during December and most likely used SSH tunnelling to obtain connectivity into the private APN.[^the-december-2025-cyberattack-on-polands-energy-sector-cert-polska-follow-up-2026]

Beginning on 18 December, the attacker scanned that APN for services including VNC, HTTP, Siemens S7, and Modbus. One of the discovered endpoints was a **WAGO PFC200 controller** associated with the second CHP plant. Its web administration interface was reachable through the APN and was configured with the default credentials for its `admin` account. The attacker appears to have used the web interface to enable SSH on the controller's WAN interface and then used another SSH tunnel to enter the CHP plant's OT network. The WAGO controller had connectivity not only to the APN but also to SCADA systems and industrial network segments containing devices responsible for important plant processes.[^the-december-2025-cyberattack-on-polands-energy-sector-cert-polska-follow-up-2026]

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-the-december-2025-cyberattack-on-polands-energy-sector-private-apn-attack-path
%%| fig-cap: "Reconstructed attack path disclosed in CERT Polska's August 2026 follow-up: compromise of a wind-farm perimeter led through a cellular router and a DSO-managed private APN to a WAGO controller at a second CHP plant, from which the attacker reached the plant's OT network and process controllers."
%%| fig-alt: "Attack-chain diagram beginning with Internet access to a compromised FortiGate VPN and firewall at a wind farm. The attacker reaches a Teltonika RUTX50 cellular router, establishes an SSH tunnel into a DSO-managed private APN, scans the APN, finds a WAGO PFC200 controller at a CHP plant, uses default administrative credentials and enables SSH, establishes a second tunnel into the CHP OT network, accesses SCADA and Siemens S7 controllers, and disrupts the steam turbine and process-water treatment system."
%%| fig-align: center
%%{init: {"theme": "neo", "look": "handDrawn", "layout": "elk"}}%%
flowchart TD
    A[Internet] --> B[Wind farm<br/>FortiGate VPN + firewall]
    B --> C[Teltonika RUTX50<br/>cellular router]
    C -->|SSH tunnel| D[DSO-managed<br/>private APN]
    D --> E[APN reconnaissance<br/>HTTP, VNC, S7, Modbus]
    E --> F[WAGO PFC200<br/>at second CHP plant]
    F --> G[Default admin credentials<br/>SSH enabled on WAN]
    G -->|SSH tunnel| H[CHP plant<br/>OT network]
    H --> I[SCADA interface]
    H --> J[Siemens S7-300<br/>S7-1200<br/>S7-1500]
    J --> K[Controllers placed in STOP mode<br/>configuration protected]
    K --> L[Steam turbine stopped<br/>water treatment stopped]
    L --> M[Cogeneration process interrupted]
```

The distinction from a direct compromise of the DSO network is important. The follow-up does **not** establish that the attacker penetrated the DSO's SCADA or corporate infrastructure. Nor does it invalidate the earlier observation that serial DNP3 connectivity can reduce the possibility of directly pivoting from a GCP into DSO systems. Instead, it exposes an orthogonal path: the attacker exploited the **field communications transport shared by multiple endpoints**. In other words, the serial boundary protected one direction of trust, while an insufficiently isolated private APN created another.

That is a much more general lesson than the particular device models involved. A private APN may provide separation from the public Internet, but **private addressing and restricted carrier access do not by themselves create endpoint isolation**. If devices attached to the APN can establish arbitrary connections to one another, then compromise of any one reachable endpoint can potentially change the security meaning of the entire network.

### Reconnaissance became direct manipulation of the physical process

Once inside the CHP plant, the attacker did not immediately begin destruction. CERT Polska reconstructed reconnaissance between 18 and 25 December. Attempts were made to authenticate to the plant's firewall and VPN gateway, but they were unsuccessful. The attacker then scanned internal subnets for industrial services including S7, Modbus, and CODESYS, as well as RDP, VNC, HTTP, HTTPS, and RTSP. In one subnet, scanning began with the address assigned to the SCADA system, which CERT Polska interprets as suggesting that the attacker may already have identified a high-value target. On 25 December, successful S7 connections were established to three Siemens PLCs; their exact purpose cannot be determined, although CERT Polska considers reconnaissance in preparation for the later disruptive actions the most likely explanation.[^the-december-2025-cyberattack-on-polands-energy-sector-cert-polska-follow-up-2026]

The destructive phase on 29 December went significantly further than the loss of telemetry documented at the renewable sites. Activity inside the CHP network began at approximately **05:30 and continued until around 10:10**. The attacker connected to the SCADA web interface and then to Siemens S7-300, S7-1200, and S7-1500 controllers. According to plant personnel, the PLCs were placed into **STOP mode** and protected with a password that prevented operators from changing their operating state or modifying the control logic. The resulting process effects were direct: the steam turbine and the water treatment system used to produce process water were shut down, interrupting the cogeneration process.[^the-december-2025-cyberattack-on-polands-energy-sector-cert-polska-follow-up-2026]

The outage remained short because plant personnel responded quickly, restoring the affected controllers to factory settings and reloading available backups. Customers did not lose heat or electricity. But the timing contains an important incident-response detail: restoration began at approximately 07:30, while the attacker appears to have remained active in the network for several more hours. The emergency recovery procedure also deleted locally stored PLC logs, limiting subsequent forensic reconstruction. This is another example of a recurring tension in OT response: **the fastest action for restoring the physical process is not always the action that best preserves evidence or assures that the adversary has actually been expelled**.[^the-december-2025-cyberattack-on-polands-energy-sector-cert-polska-follow-up-2026]

The attacker also modified **seven Moxa serial device servers and three Moxa network switches**. As in the renewable-site attacks, the devices were factory-reset, their passwords were changed, and their IP addresses were replaced with unreachable values such as `127.0.0.1`. CERT Polska assesses with high confidence that these actions were automated, based on the timing of the HTTP requests. Connections were additionally observed to two ABB ACS-series variable-frequency drives, although investigators could not establish whether configuration changes were made. Attempts to reach Schneider Electric ATV6xx drives failed because the attacker targeted the wrong TCP port.[^the-december-2025-cyberattack-on-polands-energy-sector-cert-polska-follow-up-2026]

This is significant because the new evidence crosses a boundary that the renewable attacks largely did not. At the wind and solar sites, the principal observed effect was destruction of the **coordination and telecontrol layer** while electricity generation continued. At the second CHP plant, the attacker reached controllers involved in the production process and deliberately changed their operating state. The December campaign therefore contained both forms of OT sabotage: attacks against the digital nervous system around the process and **direct manipulation of controllers capable of stopping the process itself**.

### The cleanup sequence was part of the attack

The follow-up also makes the adversary's evidence-destruction behaviour clearer. After the disruptive actions, the attacker returned to the SCADA web interface, which CERT Polska assesses was most likely an attempt to inspect the effects. The WAGO PFC200 that had served as the gateway into the CHP network was then damaged by corruption of its partition table. A subsequent factory-reset attempt by the plant could not restore the device, and laboratory examination failed to recover useful logs.[^the-december-2025-cyberattack-on-polands-energy-sector-cert-polska-follow-up-2026]

The attacker then moved backward through the same access chain. Approximately thirty minutes after the last observed activity at the CHP plant, the Teltonika router at the wind farm was factory-reset, its administrator password was changed, and its address was set to `127.0.0.1`. Finally, the wind farm's FortiGate VPN and firewall was also restored to factory settings, causing the loss of its logs. The sequence strongly reinforces a point already visible in the first report: **destruction was aimed not only at operational availability but also at restoration capability and forensic visibility**.[^the-december-2025-cyberattack-on-polands-energy-sector-cert-polska-follow-up-2026]

In this case, however, investigators recovered enough evidence from other sources to reconstruct the route. Mobile-network-operator logs, persistent data surviving on the Teltonika router, network logs inside the plant, device behaviour, and timing correlations collectively allowed CERT Polska to work backward from the physical disruption to the original wind-farm foothold. The case therefore provides a particularly concrete example of why logs required for serious OT investigation cannot reside only on the devices most likely to be reset, corrupted, replaced, or physically damaged.

### What the update changes in the architectural lesson

The strongest new lesson is that **a private APN must not be treated as a trusted extension of OT merely because it is private**. CERT Polska found that the relevant APN configuration permitted arbitrary communication between attached devices. Its subsequent surveys indicated that this type of configuration was commonly encountered among Polish users of similar services, and the team states that comparable configurations are, to the best of its knowledge, also widely deployed internationally.[^the-december-2025-cyberattack-on-polands-energy-sector-cert-polska-follow-up-2026]

CERT Polska therefore recommends client isolation between APN-connected endpoints where possible, explicit risk assessment where endpoint-to-endpoint communication is genuinely required, allowlist-based controls between the APN gateway and OT, monitoring of traffic against an expected communications profile, centralized logging, removal of unnecessary web, SSH, and Telnet administration services from APN-reachable interfaces, elimination of default credentials, and inclusion of private APNs in penetration tests, red-team exercises, and architecture reviews. Most importantly, where the organization does not control or cannot independently verify the security properties of the APN, CERT Polska recommends treating it as an **external, untrusted network with a trust level equivalent to the Internet**.[^the-december-2025-cyberattack-on-polands-energy-sector-cert-polska-follow-up-2026]

That recommendation fits directly into the architecture-first interpretation developed earlier in this article. A network's name or ownership model is not a security boundary. **Trust must follow enforceable communication properties, not topology labels.** A carrier-managed private APN, an MPLS service, a vendor VPN, a cloud private network, or another non-public transport may reduce some classes of exposure, but none should automatically confer authorization on the endpoints connected to it. The relevant questions remain the same: which identities and devices can communicate, through which interfaces, using which protocols, for which functions, under whose administration, with what logging, and with what controls if one endpoint is compromised.

The follow-up therefore strengthens rather than overturns the central thesis of the original article. The December 2025 campaign was not simply a collection of poorly hardened devices. It was an attack on **relationships between systems**: first Internet-to-perimeter, then perimeter-to-management plane, then management plane-to-cellular router, then private APN-to-field controller, and finally field controller-to-process network. Each individual connection had an operational purpose. The attack became possible because those legitimate connections composed into a path of authority that no single device description made obvious.

For distributed energy architecture, that is perhaps the most important addition to the case. The attack surface does not stop at the plant boundary, and it does not stop at the DSO-facing interface either. It includes the communications substrates through which geographically separated devices are made reachable. **If a compromise at one renewable site can be converted into network reachability toward another industrial facility through shared telecommunications infrastructure, then inter-site isolation becomes a critical-infrastructure requirement, not merely a telecom configuration preference.**

[^the-december-2025-cyberattack-on-polands-energy-sector-cert-polska-follow-up-2026]: CERT Polska. (2026, August 8). **Follow-Up Analysis of the 29 December 2025 Energy Sector Incident**. *NASK – National Research Institute*. [Report](https://cert.pl/uploads/docs/CERT_Polska_Energy_Sector_Incident_Follow_up_Report_2025.pdf)

## Appendix A — Recent European cyberattacks against energy infrastructure

The Polish incident is easier to interpret when placed beside other recent European cases. The comparison below is deliberately **selective rather than exhaustive**. It covers publicly documented incidents from 2023 to August 2026 for which sufficiently reliable evidence exists to distinguish compromise of an energy company's enterprise IT from compromise of OT, direct manipulation of an industrial process, or disruption of energy delivery.

The table now uses a single chronological list, and each incident is treated in a corresponding subsection below. One case requires an explicit scope qualification: the April 2025 Norwegian dam attack involved water-management infrastructure associated with a fish-farming facility rather than an electricity-generation asset. It is retained as an adjacent OT comparator because it provides unusually clear evidence of remote cyber manipulation producing a physical effect, but it should not be misclassified as an attack on Norwegian hydropower infrastructure.[^the-december-2025-cyberattack-on-polands-energy-sector-norway-risevatnet-dam-2025]

: Selected publicly documented European energy-sector cyber incidents, together with the adjacent Norwegian OT case, May 2023–August 2026. The comparison distinguishes enterprise-IT compromise, access to industrial environments, attempted OT disruption, and confirmed manipulation of physical processes. {#tbl-the-december-2025-cyberattack-on-polands-energy-sector-recent-european-energy-incidents}

### Denmark — coordinated compromise of energy companies, May 2023

The May 2023 Danish campaign is the closest pre-Poland example of **coordinated compromise across multiple energy operators**. SektorCERT documented attacks against 22 companies managing parts of Danish energy infrastructure; eleven were successfully compromised. Vulnerabilities in Zyxel firewalls provided the initial route into the affected environments, and SektorCERT reported access to industrial control systems at some victims. Several organisations resorted to island-mode operation during the incident or its containment.[^the-december-2025-cyberattack-on-polands-energy-sector-sektorcert-denmark-2023]

The architectural parallel with Poland is stronger than the malware comparison. In both cases, an appliance intended to enforce the boundary between an external network and operational infrastructure became a mechanism through which that boundary could collapse. The Danish campaign therefore demonstrated before December 2025 that **compromise of standardized edge infrastructure could be scaled across multiple energy operators**. What the public Danish evidence did not show was the later Polish combination of destructive field-device actions, wipers, direct PLC manipulation, and lateral movement between geographically distinct operational environments.

### Slovenia — HSE ransomware without electricity disruption, November 2023

Holding Slovenske elektrarne, Slovenia's largest electricity producer, disclosed a cyberattack against its information systems in November 2023. HSE reported that key power-plant operation systems remained operational, electricity production and trading continued, and connectivity necessary for electricity operations was maintained. Slovenia's Government Information Security Office stated that available information did not indicate a significant impact on the uninterrupted provision of essential electricity-generation and transmission services.[^the-december-2025-cyberattack-on-polands-energy-sector-hse-slovenia-2023] CERT-EU subsequently classified the incident as ransomware. ([hse.si][1])

The case illustrates why **victim sector and cyber-physical impact must be treated as separate variables**. A serious enterprise compromise at an electricity producer does not imply that the adversary obtained authority over the generation process. HSE is therefore a useful contrast with Poland: in Slovenia, the available evidence indicates that the operational boundary held; in Poland, attackers repeatedly crossed such boundaries and reached RTUs, HMIs, protection equipment, communications devices, and PLCs.

### Ukraine — FrostyGoop and district-heating disruption in Lviv, January 2024

The January 2024 incident affecting a district-energy company in Lviv is the strongest recent European comparator for **direct malicious manipulation of an industrial process**. Information shared by Ukraine's Cyber Security Situation Center with Dragos indicated that adversaries sent Modbus commands to ENCO controllers, causing incorrect measurements and system malfunction. Approximately two days of heating service were lost. Dragos assessed with moderate confidence that the FrostyGoop ICS malware was involved.[^the-december-2025-cyberattack-on-polands-energy-sector-dragos-frostygoop-ukraine-2024]

FrostyGoop is significant because its functionality was explicitly oriented toward interaction with an industrial protocol. Poland demonstrates the complementary lesson: **purpose-built ICS malware is not necessary once an attacker already possesses sufficient operational access**. At the second Polish CHP plant, legitimate Siemens S7 functionality was sufficient to place controllers into STOP mode. At renewable sites, ordinary management interfaces were sufficient to corrupt firmware, delete device files, reset equipment, and destroy HMI systems. Both incidents therefore converge on the same underlying principle: the decisive capability is the ability to issue consequential commands to an industrial function, not the sophistication of the executable carrying them.

### Romania — Electrica ransomware contained to IT, December 2024

On 9 December 2024, Electrica Group disclosed a cyberattack affecting its information infrastructure while stating that critical systems had not been affected. Romania's National Cyber Security Directorate subsequently identified the event as a **Lynx ransomware attack** and reported that, based on the information available to it, critical systems used for electricity distribution remained unaffected.[^the-december-2025-cyberattack-on-polands-energy-sector-electrica-romania-2024][^the-december-2025-cyberattack-on-polands-energy-sector-dnsc-lynx-electrica-2024] ([dnsc.ro][2])

Electrica therefore belongs primarily to the enterprise-IT end of the spectrum. The incident remained relevant to infrastructure security because compromise of corporate systems can expose credentials, maintenance information, remote-access tooling, engineering documents, configuration data, and identities useful for a later OT intrusion. The public evidence, however, does not justify promoting the incident into a case of demonstrated manipulation of electricity-control systems.

### Norway — direct manipulation of the Lake Risevatnet dam, April 2025

On 7 April 2025, attackers obtained remote control of a digital system operating a discharge valve at the Lake Risevatnet dam near Bremanger in western Norway. The valve remained fully open for approximately four hours, increasing water discharge by roughly 500 litres per second before the activity was detected and stopped. No injuries or physical damage resulted. Norwegian authorities later publicly attributed the operation to Russian or Russia-linked cyber actors.[^the-december-2025-cyberattack-on-polands-energy-sector-norway-risevatnet-dam-2025] ([Reuters][3])

Technical reporting by Claroty described a web-accessible control interface protected by weak authentication as the relevant exposure.[^the-december-2025-cyberattack-on-polands-energy-sector-norway-risevatnet-technical-2025] The incident is notable because attackers did not merely enter an organisation's network: they **changed the state of a physical actuator and altered a real process**. ([Claroty][4])

Its inclusion here nevertheless requires precision. Contemporary reporting identifies the affected installation as a dam associated with fish farming, not as an electricity-generating hydropower plant. It is therefore an adjacent critical-infrastructure comparator rather than another energy-sector victim. ([The Guardian][5]) Its relevance to the Polish analysis lies in the mechanism: an internet-reachable management surface, weak authentication, and insufficient separation between remote administration and physical control were enough to convert ordinary remote connectivity into cyber-physical authority.

### Sweden — foiled attack on a heating plant, spring 2025

In April 2026, Swedish Civil Defence Minister Carl-Oskar Bohlin publicly disclosed that a cyberattack had targeted a heating plant in western Sweden during the spring of 2025. According to the minister, the Swedish Security Service investigated the case and identified a pro-Russian actor with links to Russian intelligence and security services. The operation was intended to disrupt the facility's functioning but was stopped by an existing protection mechanism, and no serious consequences resulted.[^the-december-2025-cyberattack-on-polands-energy-sector-sweden-heating-plant-2025] ([sverigesradio.se][6])

The evidentiary limitation is as important as the incident itself. Public reporting does not provide enough technical information to reconstruct the access vector, the targeted controller architecture, or the exact actions attempted. It therefore cannot be compared technically with the Polish private-APN attack chain or FrostyGoop. What can be stated is narrower: Swedish authorities described an **attempted operation against OT responsible for a physical heating function**, and the attack failed because a protection mechanism prevented the intended consequence. ([AP News][7])

This makes Sweden a useful example of a category that is easily lost in incident statistics: **attempted cyber-physical disruption that does not become an outage**. The absence of customer impact does not imply absence of operational intent, just as the continued generation of electricity at the Polish renewable sites did not make destruction of their telecontrol infrastructure operationally irrelevant.

### Romania — Complexul Energetic Oltenia ransomware, December 2025

On 26 December 2025, only three days before the Polish campaign, Complexul Energetic Oltenia detected a ransomware attack identified as **Gentlemen** against its business IT infrastructure. Files and documents were encrypted, and several services became temporarily unavailable, including ERP, document management, email, and the company's website. Company activity was partially affected, but the operator stated that the functioning of Romania's National Energy System had not been endangered.[^the-december-2025-cyberattack-on-polands-energy-sector-oltenia-romania-2025] ([AGERPRES][8])

Recovery began on newly prepared infrastructure using available backups while investigators examined the extent of the compromise and the possibility of data exfiltration. ([AGERPRES][8]) The case is therefore useful not because it reproduces the Polish attack, but because it demonstrates the difference between **destructive enterprise impact and destructive OT impact**. Both can impose substantial recovery costs, but only the latter establishes direct adversarial authority over the energy process.

### Slovenia — Geoplin likely ransomware, January 2026

On 29 January 2026, Slovenian gas supplier Geoplin was targeted in what CERT-EU described as a likely ransomware attack. Public reporting indicated limited effects on its IT environment and alleged theft of employee, financial, and internal corporate data.[^the-december-2025-cyberattack-on-polands-energy-sector-cert-eu-geoplin-2026] ([cert.europa.eu][9])

The available evidence does **not** establish compromise of gas-control OT, manipulation of pipeline infrastructure, or interruption of gas supply. That limitation should remain explicit. Geoplin is consequently best classified as an energy-sector IT compromise with no publicly confirmed cyber-physical effect, rather than as evidence of an attack on the physical gas process.

### Romania — CONPET business-IT compromise, February 2026

On 3 February 2026, Romanian national oil-transport operator CONPET experienced a cyberattack against its business IT environment. The company's subsequent reporting stated that operational technologies were unaffected. Oil and petroleum-product transport continued, while SCADA and telecommunications systems remained operational.[^the-december-2025-cyberattack-on-polands-energy-sector-conpet-romania-2026]

CONPET completes the pattern already visible at Electrica, HSE, Geoplin, and Complexul Energetic Oltenia. Energy operators are attractive targets for conventional cybercrime and ransomware, but **compromise of an energy company should not automatically be described as compromise of energy infrastructure at the process-control level**. The distinction is particularly important when comparing such incidents with the Polish CHP plant, where attackers demonstrably reached PLCs and changed their operating state.

### Three levels of operational significance

Taken together, the cases support a useful three-level distinction.

The first level comprises **enterprise attacks against energy operators without publicly confirmed OT compromise**. HSE, Electrica, Complexul Energetic Oltenia, Geoplin, and CONPET belong principally to this category. These incidents can still be severe: corporate identity systems, engineering documents, remote-access credentials, maintenance records, backups, and supplier information may all become strategically useful to an attacker. What the evidence does not establish is direct control of the physical energy process.

The second level comprises **access to or attempted disruption of operational systems without a sustained physical service failure**. The Danish campaign crossed into ICS environments at some organisations, while the Swedish incident was explicitly described as an unsuccessful attempt to disrupt operational systems at a heating facility. The renewable component of the Polish campaign also occupies part of this middle ground: generation continued, but telemetry, remote control, protection, communications, and recovery infrastructure were deliberately damaged.

The third level comprises **confirmed manipulation of industrial functions that changes a physical process or interrupts an energy service**. The Lviv heating attack belongs clearly in this category. So does the attack against the second Polish CHP plant, where controllers were placed into STOP mode and cogeneration was interrupted. The Norwegian dam incident demonstrates the same cyber-physical transition in an adjacent water-management domain: remote access became authority over an actuator, and a digital command produced measurable physical change.

This taxonomy is more informative than simply counting "energy cyberattacks". From an architectural perspective, the significant variable is **how far through the cyber-physical stack the adversary progressed**: from enterprise data, to identities and management systems, to OT networks, to control devices, to process authority, and finally to observable physical consequences.

### Why the Polish campaign remains unusual

The broader European record shows that few of the individual ingredients observed in Poland were unprecedented. Vulnerable perimeter appliances had already enabled coordinated compromise across Danish energy organisations. Ransomware had repeatedly affected European electricity, gas, and oil companies. Ukraine had already demonstrated direct malicious use of an industrial protocol to interrupt heating. Norway had shown that weakly protected remote control could produce immediate physical manipulation, while Sweden disclosed an attempted attack explicitly intended to disrupt heating-plant OT.

What distinguishes the Polish campaign is their **composition within one coordinated operation**. The attacker acted across dozens of distributed renewable sites, destroyed heterogeneous OT equipment, compromised enterprise and Active Directory environments, deployed wipers, attempted lower-level storage destruction, directly stopped PLCs at a CHP plant, and — as CERT Polska's follow-up established — converted a compromised renewable site and a DSO-managed private APN into a lateral path toward another industrial facility.

The comparison therefore reinforces rather than dilutes the central thesis of this article. Recent European experience does not support a model in which destructive capability depends primarily on increasingly exotic "cyber weapons". The recurrent mechanisms are more ordinary: perimeter appliances, weak identities, remote administration, management interfaces, insufficient segmentation, industrial protocols, shared communications networks, and fragile recovery paths. The strategic effect depends on **which legitimate relationships those compromised components allow an attacker to traverse**.

### A useful exclusion: the April 2025 Iberian blackout

One highly visible European energy event should remain outside the table. The electricity blackout affecting Spain and Portugal on **28 April 2025** generated immediate speculation about cyberattack, but the investigation presented by the Spanish government in June found **no evidence that a cyber incident or cyberattack caused the crisis**, whether at the system operator, control centres, or generation facilities.[^the-december-2025-cyberattack-on-polands-energy-sector-spain-blackout-2025] ([La Moncloa][10])

The investigation instead described a multifactorial electrical-system failure involving oscillations, insufficient dynamic voltage-control capability, voltage increases, and generation disconnections. ([La Moncloa][10]) Its exclusion illustrates the same evidentiary discipline used throughout this appendix: **an operational failure, an attack claim, and a technically established cyberattack are different things**. Unexplained physical disruption should be investigated for malicious causes when circumstances justify it, as CERT Polska did with the second CHP plant, but it should enter a cyberattack chronology only when evidence supports that classification.
