## Appendix B — How the European Union is responding

The Polish campaign exposes four different security problems at once: **how energy operators govern cyber risk; how electricity-sector actors secure interconnected operational systems; how manufacturers design and maintain the products deployed inside those systems; and how Europe manages strategic dependence on technology suppliers**. The European Union is increasingly addressing these as separate but interacting regulatory layers.

That distinction matters because no single instrument would have covered the entire Polish attack path. NIS2 regulates the cybersecurity governance of covered organisations. The Network Code on Cybersecurity adds rules specific to the interconnected electricity system. The Cyber Resilience Act changes the product-security baseline for hardware and software placed on the Union market. The proposed revision of the Cybersecurity Act, usually referred to as **CSA2**, would add a more explicitly strategic layer for ICT supply-chain risk and high-risk suppliers.[^the-december-2025-cyberattack-on-polands-energy-sector-eu-regulatory-layers]

| EU instrument                 | Primary object of regulation                                                                      | Relevance to the Polish failure modes                                                                                              | Status in August 2026                                                                              |
| ----------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| NIS2                          | Covered essential and important entities                                                          | Governance, risk management, supply-chain security, incident handling, business continuity, management accountability, supervision | In force; national implementation remains uneven                                                   |
| Network Code on Cybersecurity | Cybersecurity of cross-border electricity flows and identified high- and critical-impact entities | Electricity-sector risk assessment, common controls, reporting, crisis management, supply-chain and substation-security measures   | In force; detailed methodologies and implementation work continue                                  |
| Cyber Resilience Act          | Products with digital elements placed on the EU market and their manufacturers                    | Secure defaults, attack-surface reduction, vulnerability handling, updates, product support, security documentation and reporting  | In force; Article 14 reporting starts 11 September 2026; general application from 11 December 2027 |
| Proposed Cybersecurity Act 2  | EU cybersecurity governance, certification and ICT supply-chain security                          | Strategic supplier dependence, high-risk suppliers and potentially critical equipment used by energy operators                     | Commission proposal; not yet enacted                                                               |

: The EU response operates at distinct but complementary levels: organisational governance, electricity-sector operation, product security, and strategic ICT supply-chain risk. {#tbl-the-december-2025-cyberattack-on-polands-energy-sector-eu-response-layers}

The importance of this architecture is that the four layers regulate **different objects**. A secure product does not guarantee a secure plant. A well-governed plant cannot compensate indefinitely for products that ship with avoidable vulnerabilities or weak lifecycle support. Sector-specific electricity rules cannot determine the security posture of every commercial product in the supply chain. And technical certification alone cannot answer geopolitical questions about structural dependence on suppliers subject to foreign control. The direction of EU policy is therefore toward overlapping controls rather than one universal cybersecurity regime.

### NIS2: moving cybersecurity into management accountability

NIS2 is the broad organisational layer. Directive (EU) 2022/2555 covers energy as a sector of high criticality and requires covered essential and important entities to implement proportionate cybersecurity risk-management measures. Those measures expressly include incident handling, business continuity and crisis management, supply-chain security, vulnerability handling, security in acquisition and development, assessment of control effectiveness, cyber hygiene, cryptography, access control, asset management, and multifactor or continuous authentication where appropriate.[^the-december-2025-cyberattack-on-polands-energy-sector-nis2-directive]

For the argument developed in this article, Article 20 is particularly important. NIS2 requires the **management bodies** of essential and important entities to approve cybersecurity risk-management measures and oversee their implementation. Member States must also ensure that management bodies can be held accountable for infringements of the relevant risk-management obligations under national law.[^the-december-2025-cyberattack-on-polands-energy-sector-nis2-directive] Cybersecurity is therefore no longer framed only as a matter delegated to an IT or OT security function. Decisions about remote access, supplier connectivity, shared credentials, recovery capability, network architecture, maintenance arrangements, and operational dependencies become governance questions for which senior management has an explicit regulatory role.

The supply-chain provision maps especially closely to the Polish case. Article 21 requires entities to address security aspects of their relationships with **direct suppliers and service providers**.[^the-december-2025-cyberattack-on-polands-energy-sector-nis2-supply-chain] That is relevant to architectures in which EPCs, telecontrol integrators, equipment manufacturers, O&M contractors, telecommunications providers, and grid operators all participate in the operational trust graph. NIS2 does not prescribe one technical topology for those relationships, but it removes any defensible assumption that third-party connectivity sits outside the regulated risk-management perimeter.

NIS2 also establishes a staged reporting regime for significant incidents: an early warning must ordinarily be submitted within 24 hours of awareness, followed by an incident notification within 72 hours and a final report normally within one month.[^the-december-2025-cyberattack-on-polands-energy-sector-nis2-reporting] The second Polish CHP incident illustrates why this matters operationally. The event was initially interpreted as a contractor error during maintenance and was reported only for informational purposes; CERT Polska's awareness of the simultaneous attacks led investigators to reconsider it as potentially malicious. A mature reporting regime therefore has to capture not only obvious ransomware events but operational anomalies whose cyber origin may initially be uncertain.

The weakness is implementation uniformity. Member States were required to transpose NIS2 by **17 October 2024**, but the deadline did not produce simultaneous national implementation.[^the-december-2025-cyberattack-on-polands-energy-sector-nis2-transposition-deadline] ECSO's tracker currently records primary transposition legislation in 23 of 27 Member States and documents material differences in scope, registration, supervision, deadlines, and implementation details.[^the-december-2025-cyberattack-on-polands-energy-sector-ecso-nis2-tracker] The Commission applies a stricter completion test: as recently as July 2026 it referred **Ireland, Spain, France, and the Netherlands** to the Court of Justice for failure to notify complete NIS2 transposition.[^the-december-2025-cyberattack-on-polands-energy-sector-nis2-july-2026-referrals]

This does not make NIS2 ineffective, but it means that an operator managing similar assets across several Member States can still encounter different national implementation conditions. The regulatory objective is a high **common** level of cybersecurity; the present implementation landscape has not yet completely achieved the common part.

### The Network Code on Cybersecurity: translating cybersecurity into electricity-system rules

NIS2 is cross-sectoral. Electricity also has a dedicated instrument: **Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1366**, the Network Code on sector-specific rules for cybersecurity aspects of cross-border electricity flows. The Regulation entered into force on 13 June 2024 and establishes a recurrent framework covering cybersecurity risk assessment, common minimum requirements, monitoring, reporting, crisis management, and other measures related to the security of the interconnected electricity system.[^the-december-2025-cyberattack-on-polands-energy-sector-nccs-regulation]

The Network Code is important because it treats cybersecurity not merely as enterprise security inside electricity companies, but as a property of **system interdependence**. ENTSO-E describes its purpose as establishing a European standard for cybersecurity of cross-border electricity flows, including cyber-risk assessment, common requirements, certification-related provisions, monitoring, reporting and crisis management.[^the-december-2025-cyberattack-on-polands-energy-sector-nccs-entsoe]

That perspective closely matches the lesson of the CERT Polska follow-up. The most consequential boundary was not necessarily the corporate perimeter of one plant. It was the relationship among a compromised GCP, a cellular router, a DSO-managed private APN, another field endpoint, and the OT network of a separate CHP plant. The Network Code's system-level approach is therefore directionally aligned with the problem demonstrated in Poland: **security has to be assessed across dependencies and communications relationships, not only asset by asset**.

Implementation is also becoming progressively more concrete. ENTSO-E and the EU DSO Entity have been developing methodologies and supporting documents under the Regulation, including cybersecurity risk-assessment methodologies, a cyberattack classification scale, minimum and advanced controls, and procurement recommendations for substation gateways.[^the-december-2025-cyberattack-on-polands-energy-sector-nccs-entsoe] The latter is particularly relevant to an incident in which routers, gateways, VPN appliances, RTUs, serial servers, and other substation-edge components were central to both compromise and recovery.

The scope should nevertheless not be overstated. The Network Code is concerned specifically with cybersecurity aspects of **cross-border electricity flows** and uses risk-based processes to identify high-impact and critical-impact entities and processes. It is not a general cybersecurity code automatically governing every wind turbine, photovoltaic inverter, PLC, BESS controller, or industrial network in Europe. Its significance lies in creating a sector-specific control layer where cyber risk can propagate into the interconnected electricity system.

### The Cyber Resilience Act: shifting part of the burden back to the product

The Cyber Resilience Act addresses a different failure mode. Regulation (EU) 2024/2847 establishes horizontal cybersecurity requirements for **products with digital elements** made available on the Union market.[^the-december-2025-cyberattack-on-polands-energy-sector-cra-regulation] As discussed in my separate analysis of the CRA, its structural innovation is to move part of cybersecurity from procurement clauses and operator hardening into product law: an in-scope manufacturer must connect cybersecurity risk assessment, secure design, vulnerability handling, conformity assessment, technical documentation, support, and market surveillance to the product that it places on the market.[^the-december-2025-cyberattack-on-polands-energy-sector-cra-longform]

This is directly relevant to several Polish attack mechanisms, but with an important qualification. It would be incorrect to claim, without product-by-product legal analysis, that every firewall, router, RTU, PLC, relay, HMI package, or serial device server appearing in the CERT Polska reports is necessarily subject to the CRA in exactly the same way. Scope depends on the statutory product definition, market placement, intended or reasonably foreseeable connectivity, applicable exclusions, product classification, and the relevant transition rules.[^the-december-2025-cyberattack-on-polands-energy-sector-cra-regulation]

The direction of the requirements is nevertheless clear. For in-scope products, Annex I establishes risk-based cybersecurity properties including secure-by-default configuration where applicable, protection against unauthorised access, attack-surface limitation, protection of availability, security-relevant monitoring, and the ability to address vulnerabilities through security updates. Manufacturers also have continuing vulnerability-handling obligations covering identification and documentation of vulnerabilities and components, testing, remediation, coordinated vulnerability disclosure, secure update distribution, and support-period management.[^the-december-2025-cyberattack-on-polands-energy-sector-cra-regulation]

Those requirements correspond strikingly with recurring weaknesses in the Polish case: default credentials, unnecessary management services, weak update integrity, exposed administrative interfaces, vulnerable firmware, long-lived industrial products, and devices whose compromise or destruction significantly complicated restoration. The CRA cannot prescribe the network architecture of a CHP plant, but it can change the security baseline of the products from which that architecture is assembled.

The timing is equally important. The CRA entered into force on 10 December 2024, but its main product obligations apply generally from **11 December 2027**. Article 14 reporting obligations apply earlier, from **11 September 2026**, requiring manufacturers to report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe security incidents affecting in-scope products according to the Regulation's notification process.[^the-december-2025-cyberattack-on-polands-energy-sector-cra-implementation-2026] The December 2025 Polish incident should therefore not be described as a failure of CRA enforcement: the Regulation's general product-security regime was not yet applicable. Its relevance is prospective. It is part of the EU response intended to make comparable device-level weaknesses less acceptable in products entering the future European market.

For industrial infrastructure, lifecycle duration is particularly consequential. The CRA links vulnerability handling to a manufacturer-defined support period based on expected use, subject to statutory minimum rules. That matters for equipment expected to remain installed for many years, because a plant's operational lifetime can substantially exceed ordinary consumer or enterprise IT refresh cycles.[^the-december-2025-cyberattack-on-polands-energy-sector-cra-longform] Product procurement will therefore increasingly need to treat cybersecurity support horizon, update architecture, dependency support, and recovery capability as engineering characteristics rather than after-sales conveniences.

### CSA2: from product security to strategic supplier risk

The proposed revision of the Cybersecurity Act adds another dimension. On 20 January 2026, the Commission proposed a new Cybersecurity Act — commonly called **CSA2** — that would replace Regulation (EU) 2019/881, reinforce ENISA and the European cybersecurity certification framework, and establish a **trusted ICT supply-chain security framework**.[^the-december-2025-cyberattack-on-polands-energy-sector-csa2-proposal]

The distinction from the CRA is fundamental. The CRA asks whether a product and its manufacturer satisfy cybersecurity obligations. CSA2's proposed supply-chain mechanism also addresses **non-technical and strategic risk associated with suppliers and third countries**. Under the Commission proposal, coordinated Union-level assessments could identify key ICT assets, countries presenting structural cybersecurity concerns, and suppliers considered high risk. Implementing measures could then restrict specified NIS2 entities from using, installing, or integrating relevant ICT components from designated high-risk suppliers, with transition periods and mitigation measures forming part of the mechanism.[^the-december-2025-cyberattack-on-polands-energy-sector-csa2-supply-chain]

Energy is not incidental to that debate. The Commission's 2026 Strategic Roadmap for Digitalisation and AI in the Energy Sector explicitly points to the proposed Cybersecurity Act as a framework that could, where necessary, support restrictions on **inverters from high-risk suppliers**.[^the-december-2025-cyberattack-on-polands-energy-sector-energy-roadmap-csa2] That is a significant shift in regulatory logic. Security assessment would no longer concern only whether an inverter, gateway, router, or software component meets technical requirements; it could also concern whether strategic dependence on its supplier creates an unacceptable systemic risk.

The connection to Poland is not that CERT Polska attributed the compromised equipment to "high-risk suppliers" in the CSA2 sense. It did not. The relevance is architectural. Modern energy systems can standardize the same vendors, firmware families, management planes, remote services, cellular equipment, and administrative models across thousands of geographically distributed assets. That standardization improves efficiency, but it can also create **concentration risk**. A vulnerability, supplier compromise, remote-management dependency, or politically unacceptable external influence can then propagate through an installed fleet rather than remain local to one plant.

The proposed framework remains exactly that — **a proposal**. It is proceeding through the ordinary EU legislative process and may change materially before adoption.[^the-december-2025-cyberattack-on-polands-energy-sector-csa2-proposal] It should therefore not yet be treated as a binding power to exclude vendors from European energy infrastructure. The more defensible conclusion is that EU policy has moved from discussing supply-chain risk principally as an operator risk-management problem toward considering an EU-level mechanism capable of imposing coordinated restrictions on strategically risky ICT suppliers.

### What the four layers achieve together

The emerging EU framework can be understood as four complementary control surfaces:

1. **NIS2 acts on the operator.** It asks whether the organisation governing the plant understands its cyber risks, controls suppliers, manages incidents, provides continuity and recovery, and makes management accountable.

2. **The Network Code acts on the electricity-system relationship.** It asks how cyber risk affects interconnected electricity operations, which processes and entities are high impact, which controls and reporting mechanisms are required, and how risk should be coordinated across TSOs, DSOs, authorities and other actors.

3. **The CRA acts on the product.** It asks whether connected hardware and software are designed, supplied, documented, updated and supported according to a legally enforceable cybersecurity baseline.

4. **CSA2, if adopted substantially in the form proposed, would act on strategic supply dependence.** It would create mechanisms through which technically functional ICT components could nevertheless become unacceptable for certain critical uses because of broader supply-chain and third-country risk.

This layered response is directionally consistent with the architecture-first argument of this article. The Polish attack succeeded because individually legitimate relationships — remote VPN access, firewall administration, device-management interfaces, cellular connectivity, a private APN, field controllers, Windows domains, vendor access, and recovery mechanisms — composed into paths that an attacker could traverse. The EU response increasingly regulates **the actors, products, relationships, and dependencies from which those paths are built**.

But regulation cannot remove the design problem. NIS2 can make management responsible for risk without deciding the correct VLAN, conduit, jump-host, or maintenance architecture for a particular plant. The Network Code can define common electricity-sector requirements without hardening every field device. The CRA can require a better product baseline without preventing an operator from deploying a secure product in an insecure topology. CSA2 may eventually reduce certain strategic supplier dependencies without eliminating vulnerabilities in trusted suppliers. And none of these instruments can substitute for tested restoration, offline configuration backups, protected logs, site-specific credentials, constrained management planes, inter-site isolation, or disciplined commissioning.

The strongest reading of the EU response is therefore not that **compliance will prevent the next Poland**. It is that European law is progressively making the architectural shortcuts exposed by Poland harder to justify. Weak product defaults become a manufacturer problem. Uncontrolled supplier relationships become an operator-governance problem. Cross-border electricity dependencies become a sector-level risk problem. Concentration in strategically risky suppliers may become a Union-level supply-chain problem.

That is an important change in the allocation of responsibility. The old model allowed insecurity to fall between contracts: the manufacturer supplied a configurable product, the integrator installed it, the operator accepted it, the telecom provider connected it, and each party could plausibly regard the remaining risk as someone else's problem. The emerging European framework increasingly removes those gaps.

The remaining task is technical rather than legislative: **turn the overlapping legal obligations into one coherent architecture before the plant is commissioned**. That means using product assurance, enterprise architecture, IEC 62443 zones and conduits, identity governance, supplier controls, communications isolation, evidence collection, and recovery engineering as parts of the same design process. The Polish campaign demonstrates what happens when operational connectivity is allowed to compose faster than security governance. The EU response is increasingly designed to make that condition legally, economically, and operationally more difficult to sustain.
